drills.q: Name the four resilience primitives and their job.
drills.a: Timeout bounds one call, retry recovers transient faults, circuit breaker stops calls to a failing dependency, and bulkhead limits concurrent damage to the caller.

drills.q: Why must retry require a timeout?
drills.a: Without a timeout, one attempt can wait indefinitely and consume the caller's resources; retry then compounds unbounded latency and concurrency pressure.

drills.q: Why should the breaker usually see one outcome for a retry group?
drills.a: Three retry attempts are one logical dependency call. Counting each attempt as a separate breaker failure trips the breaker faster than the business-level failure rate justifies.

drills.q: What is full jitter protecting against?
drills.a: It randomizes retry delays so clients that observed the same outage do not wake and retry in synchrony, avoiding a thundering herd during recovery.

drills.q: Why can a circuit breaker stay closed while the service is already hurting users?
drills.a: A failure-only breaker ignores slow successful calls. Configure slow-call thresholds or latency-based signals so degraded responses can trip protection before outright errors arrive.

drills.q: What does a bulkhead reject, and why should it reject immediately?
drills.a: It rejects new work when the dependency's concurrency capacity is full. Immediate rejection prevents an unbounded queue from converting downstream slowness into caller-wide thread or task exhaustion.

drills.q: How do you size a bulkhead starting from measurements?
drills.a: Use Little's Law: concurrency is approximately throughput multiplied by latency, then add a bounded safety factor and validate against saturation and tail latency rather than choosing a number by intuition.

drills.q: Which errors should not trip a breaker?
drills.a: Business or expected errors such as a 404 or validation rejection. Classify exceptions explicitly so the breaker represents dependency health, not normal application semantics.

drills.q: Why propagate an absolute deadline instead of a fresh timeout at each layer?
drills.a: An absolute deadline preserves the remaining end-to-end budget across nested calls. Fresh per-layer timeouts can let inner work consume the entire user-facing SLO before an outer fallback runs.

drills.q: What is a common breaker-keying mistake?
drills.a: Creating one breaker per fully parameterized URL or request ID. Key by service and route template so each breaker gets enough observations without merging unrelated failure domains.
